mainTopic: Which sensitive passages are read and translated, read but not translated, or not read at all; polite substitutes for crude words; mocking עבודה זרה; and the start of פרק בני העיר.
overview: This amud goes through a list of embarrassing passages in תנ"ך and rules on how each is handled in the public reading. First comes a ברייתא of passages that are read and translated: לוט and his daughters, תמר and יהודה, the first account of the עגל, the קללות and ברכות, the אזהרות and עונשין, אמנון and תמר, אבשלום, פילגש בגבעה, and יחזקאל's rebuke of ירושלים. For almost every item the גמרא asks 'פשיטא!' and answers 'מהו דתימא': we might have worried about someone's honor or the listeners' feelings, and the ruling rejects that worry. For יחזקאל's rebuke, the ruling instead comes to reject רבי אליעזר, who objected to reading it. Next comes the list of רעבד"ן, passages that are read but not translated: ראובן, the second account of the עגל (where אהרן's careless words gave the מינין an opening), and ברכת כהנים, because of the word 'ישא'. The story of דוד and אמנון is not even read; the גמרא explains that this applies only to verses that say 'אמנון בן דוד'. A ברייתא then teaches that crude words are read with polite substitutes, and רב נחמן and others rule that mocking עבודה זרה is the one kind of mockery that is permitted. The פרק ends with a הדרן, and a new פרק opens with a משנה teaching that money from selling a holy item may only buy something holier.

steps.title: Finishing the point about reading the Creation story in public
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of the answer about מעשה בראשית. Even though people might come to ask what came before Creation and what will come after, the ברייתא teaches that it is still read in public.
steps.simpleTranslation: ...and what is before and what is after. Therefore the ברייתא teaches us that it is still read.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a sentence from the previous section. It had been explaining why we might have thought מעשה בראשית should not be read publicly, and now it closes with 'קא משמע לן': the ברייתא teaches that it is read anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier worry was that hearing the Creation story would lead people to ask improper questions, such as what existed 'before' Creation and what will be 'after' the end of time. The ברייתא's ruling tells us this worry does not stop the public reading. This 'מהו דתימא / קא משמע לן' structure is the template for every step that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: The account of Creation at the start of the Torah
After (here: what will be at the end of time)
'It teaches us': the new point the source is coming to tell us

phrases.english: and what is before and what is after,
phrases.notes: This picks up the worry from the previous amud: people would start asking what came before Creation and what comes after.

phrases.english: it teaches us (that it is read anyway).
phrases.notes: This wraps up the 'מהו דתימא' (you might have thought) answer that started earlier.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer earlier about מעשה בראשית.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: a plausible concern is raised and then dismissed by the ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Perhaps מעשה בראשית should not be read publicly, because it may lead people to ask what came before and after Creation.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא teaches that it is read in public anyway.

steps.title: The story of לוט and his daughters is read and translated
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that the incident of לוט and his two daughters is read in the Torah reading and translated into Aramaic for the congregation.
steps.simpleTranslation: The incident of לוט and his two daughters is read and translated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next item on the ברייתא's list. The story of לוט and his daughters is both read and translated publicly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the times of the גמרא, a מתורגמן translated each verse of the Torah reading into Aramaic so that everyone would understand. Some embarrassing passages were read but not translated. This ruling puts the לוט story in the category of passages that are fully read and translated.

keyTerms.meaning: אברהם's nephew, whose daughters had relations with him (בראשית 19)
It is read (in the public Torah reading)
And it is translated (into Aramaic for the congregation)
The translator who rendered the Torah reading into Aramaic aloud

phrases.english: The incident of Lot and his two daughters
phrases.notes: From בראשית 19:30–38.
Both read from the Torah and translated aloud into Aramaic.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַעֲשֵׂה לוֹט וּשְׁתֵּי בְנוֹתָיו נִקְרָא וּמִתַּרְגֵּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next item in the ברייתא's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The story of לוט and his daughters is read publicly and translated.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that this ruling seems obvious. Why would anyone think otherwise?
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא for stating something that seems too obvious to need saying. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The assumption is that a ברייתא should not waste words teaching what everyone already knows. Unlike the עגל, the לוט story is not about a sin of כלל ישראל, so why would we hesitate to translate it? The גמרא wants to find what new point the ruling teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is obvious!': a challenge that a statement teaches nothing new

phrases.notes: Just one word, but it's a full challenge all by itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the necessity of the ruling in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the לוט story is read and translated.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: There seems to be no reason to hold back this story, so stating the ruling looks unnecessary.

steps.title: We might have worried about אברהם's honor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that we might have avoided translating the story out of respect for אברהם, since לוט was his nephew. The ברייתא teaches that this is not a concern.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: let us be concerned for the honor of אברהם. So it teaches us that we do not hold back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the ruling is not obvious. Someone might have thought the story shames אברהם through his relative, so the ברייתא needed to say it is still read and translated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The hidden worry is family honor. לוט's disgrace could reflect badly on his uncle אברהם. The ברייתא rejects this: a relative's embarrassment is not a reason to hide a passage of Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What might you have said?': introduces a reasonable mistaken assumption

phrases.notes: Here comes what we might have wrongly thought, the הוה אמינא.

phrases.english: let us be concerned for the honor of Avraham,
phrases.notes: לוט was אברהם's nephew.

phrases.english: so it teaches us (that we do not hold back).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: identifies a plausible concern that the ruling rejects
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Do not translate the story, out of respect for אברהם.
steps.terutzMaskana: אברהם's honor is not a reason to hold the story back; it is read and translated.

steps.title: The story of תמר and יהודה is read and translated
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that the incident of תמר and יהודה is read and translated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The incident of תמר and יהודה is read and translated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next item on the ברייתא's list: the story of יהודה and תמר is read and translated publicly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this story (בראשית 38), יהודה unknowingly had relations with his daughter-in-law תמר. It is an embarrassing episode about one of the שבטים, the ancestor of מלכות בית דוד. The ruling still puts it among the passages that are fully read and translated.

keyTerms.meaning: One of the twelve שבטים, son of יעקב

phrases.english: The incident of Tamar and Yehudah
phrases.notes: בראשית 38.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the same ברייתא list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The story of תמר and יהודה is read publicly and translated.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious too?
steps.stepSummary: The same challenge again: the ruling seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats its challenge, asking why the ברייתא needs to tell us this. It is setting up another 'you might have thought' answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא applies the same test to each item in the list. Each ruling must teach something that is not self-evident.

keyTerms.meaning: A new point or novelty that a ruling teaches

phrases.notes: The same challenge as in step 3.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the necessity of the ruling in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the תמר and יהודה story is read and translated.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: There seems to be no reason to hold it back, so the statement looks unnecessary.

steps.title: יהודה's honor is not hurt: the story praises him for confessing
steps.stepSummary: We might have worried about יהודה's honor. The ברייתא teaches that the story is actually to his credit, because he admitted his mistake.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: let us be concerned for the honor of יהודה. So it teaches us that it is his praise, for he confessed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the ruling was needed: one might have hidden the story to protect יהודה. The answer goes further and says the story actually praises him, because he publicly admitted 'צדקה ממני'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer is stronger than the one about לוט. There, the worry was simply set aside. Here, the worry is turned upside down: יהודה's honest confession makes the story a source of honor, so there is nothing to hide.

keyTerms.meaning: 'She is more righteous than I': יהודה's admission (בראשית 38:26)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that admitting a wrong publicly is something praiseworthy, worthy of being read aloud in shul, not a source of shame.

phrases.english: let us be concerned for the honor of Yehudah,
that it is his praise, for he confessed.
phrases.notes: Refers to 'צדקה ממני'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge of step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא, with the concern reversed into praise
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Do not translate the story, to protect יהודה's honor.
steps.terutzMaskana: The story is to יהודה's credit because he confessed, so it is read and translated.

steps.title: The first account of the Golden Calf is read and translated
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that the first account of the עגל episode is read and translated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The first incident of the Calf is read and translated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next item: the first part of the עגל story is read and translated publicly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The עגל was כלל ישראל's most notorious sin. 'The first' refers to the opening account of the sin itself, as opposed to a later section that is treated differently. This passage is fully read and translated despite its shameful content.

keyTerms.meaning: The first (account): the opening narrative of the sin

steps.confusionAlert: 'עגל הראשון' does not mean there were two calves. It means the first account of the incident. The משנה (25a), and the ברייתא later on this amud (steps 29–31), contrast it with the 'second account' about אהרן's role, which is read but not translated.

phrases.english: The first incident of the Calf
phrases.notes: The opening account in שמות 32.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the ברייתא list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first account of the עגל is read publicly and translated.

steps.title: Isn't this also obvious?
steps.stepSummary: Once more the גמרא challenges: why must this be stated?
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא again asks why the ruling is needed. It is setting up the final 'you might have thought' answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same pattern repeats a third time. The גמרא assumes there must be a hidden reason someone would have refrained.

keyTerms.meaning: The sin of the Golden Calf

phrases.notes: The same challenge as in steps 3 and 6.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the necessity of the ruling in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the first account of the עגל is read and translated.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: There seems to be no reason to hold back a Torah passage, so the ruling looks unnecessary.

steps.title: The shame of the עגל actually brings ישראל atonement
steps.stepSummary: We might have worried about the honor of ישראל. The ברייתא teaches that they are all the more pleased by it, because the public embarrassment brings them כפרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: let us be concerned for the honor of ישראל. So it teaches us: all the more so is it pleasing to them, since it becomes an atonement for them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that one might have hidden the עגל story to protect כלל ישראל's dignity. The answer is that the public reading is welcome to them, because the embarrassment itself serves as כפרה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the יהודה answer, this one flips the concern. The shame is not a reason to hide the story; it is the very thing that helps atone for the sin. So reading it aloud benefits ישראל rather than harming them.

keyTerms.meaning: The honor of the Jewish people
It is pleasing / acceptable to them

steps.whatToRemember: All three cases follow the same pattern: 'נקרא ומתרגם', then 'פשיטא!', then 'מהו דתימא ... קא משמע לן'. For לוט, the worry about אברהם's honor is simply dismissed. For יהודה and the עגל, the supposed shame turns out to be a benefit: praise for confessing, and כפרה through embarrassment.
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches the principle that public embarrassment over a sin can itself be part of the atonement process. That is why even כלל ישראל's worst moment is read aloud and translated.

phrases.english: let us be concerned for the honor of Israel,
all the more so is it pleasing to them,
phrases.notes: They prefer that it be publicized.

phrases.english: since it becomes an atonement for them.
phrases.notes: The shame of the public reading brings atonement.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: לֵיחוּשׁ לִכְבוֹדָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge of step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא, with the concern reversed into a benefit
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Do not translate the עגל story, to protect the honor of ישראל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The public shame brings כפרה, so ישראל are all the more pleased that it is read and translated.

steps.title: The curses and blessings are read and translated
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that the sections of קללות and ברכות are read in public and translated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The curses and the blessings are read and translated.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives its next ruling: the Torah sections with the blessings and the curses are read aloud and translated for the people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are the long sections in פרשת בחוקותי and פרשת כי תבוא that describe rewards and frightening punishments. The ruling is that they are not skipped and not left untranslated.

keyTerms.meaning: Curses. Here, the Torah's sections of punishment (the תוכחה).
Blessings. The rewards promised alongside the curses.
They are read aloud from the Torah in public.
They are translated into Aramaic for the listeners by the מתורגמן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the same list of the ברייתא, after the עגל ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The sections of קללות and ברכות are read and translated in public.

steps.title: Why is this ruling needed at all
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: this is obvious, so why state it?
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks again why the ברייתא needs to tell us this. Of course a Torah section is read and translated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The default is that every part of the Torah is read and translated. A ruling that only repeats the default seems unnecessary, so the גמרא wants to know what new point it teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is obvious!' A challenge that a ruling teaches nothing new.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the ruling in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that קללות and ברכות are read and translated.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Reading and translating the Torah is the normal practice, so stating it seems unnecessary.

steps.title: We might have worried about upsetting the congregation
steps.stepSummary: We might have thought the frightening curses would upset the ציבור. The ברייתא teaches that they are read anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: let us worry that perhaps the congregation will become upset. So it teaches us that they are read.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the new point. Hearing so many curses could make the ציבור upset or discouraged, so we might have skipped them. The ברייתא tells us not to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is about how the listeners will feel. The ברייתא answers that this worry does not override the duty to read and translate the Torah's sections.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You might have said.' Introduces a mistaken assumption that the ruling comes to reject.
Their minds will become upset or discouraged.
'It teaches us.' Shows that the ruling rejects the mistaken assumption.

phrases.english: let us be concerned that perhaps will become upset

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא נֵיחוּשׁ דִּלְמָא פָּיְיגָא דַּעְתַּיְיהוּ דְצִבּוּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא of step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: identifies a possible worry that the ruling rejects.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The curses might be skipped so the ציבור does not become upset.
steps.terutzMaskana: They are read and translated despite the worry.

steps.title: The warnings and punishments are read and translated
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that the Torah's warnings and punishments are read and translated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The warnings and the punishments are read and translated.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives its next ruling: the passages that warn against sins and state their punishments are read and translated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These passages list prohibitions together with the punishment for breaking them. The ruling is that they are presented to the public like any other section.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the ברייתא's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אזהרות and עונשין are read and translated.

steps.title: Again, why is this needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא again asks why such an obvious ruling is stated.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The same challenge comes up again: of course these Torah passages are read and translated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא wants to find the specific worry that this ruling removes.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling on אזהרות and עונשין.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Reading and translating is the default, so the ruling seems unnecessary.

steps.title: We might have worried people would serve ה׳ only out of fear
steps.stepSummary: We might have worried that people would keep the מצוות only out of fear of punishment. The ברייתא teaches that the passages are read anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: let us worry that perhaps people will come to act out of fear. So it teaches us that they are read.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the new point. Hearing the punishments might lead people to keep the מצוות only because they are afraid. The ברייתא says we still read and translate them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ideal is to serve ה׳ out of love. The worry was that stressing punishment would lower people to service based on fear. The ברייתא rules that this is not a reason to hide these passages.

keyTerms.meaning: Out of fear of punishment, not out of love.

phrases.english: let us be concerned that perhaps they will come

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא נֵיחוּשׁ דִּלְמָא אָתוּ לְמֶעְבַּד מִיִּרְאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: identifies a possible worry that the ruling rejects.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Hide the punishments so that people serve ה׳ out of love, not fear.
steps.terutzMaskana: They are read and translated anyway.

steps.title: The stories of אמנון and תמר, and of אבשלום, are read and translated
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that the stories of אמנון and תמר and of אבשלום are read and translated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The story of אמנון and תמר is read and translated. The story of אבשלום is read and translated.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא moves to painful stories in נביאים about דוד's children and rules that they are read and translated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These stories in ספר שמואל ב are אמנון's crime against his sister תמר and אבשלום's rebellion against his father דוד. The ruling is that they are not hidden from the public.

keyTerms.meaning: דוד's son who violated his half-sister תמר.
דוד's son who rebelled against him.

steps.confusionAlert: The words in square brackets about אבשלום are a textual addition found in some versions. They are still part of this text, and the ruling about them is the same.

phrases.english: The incident of Amnon and Tamar

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the list, moving from Torah passages to נביאים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The stories of אמנון and תמר and of אבשלום are read and translated.

steps.title: Why state this about דוד's family
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: this is obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: Once again the גמרא asks why this needs to be said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like every other passage of תנ"ך, these stories should simply be read. The גמרא looks for the worry that made the ruling necessary.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling on אמנון, תמר, and אבשלום.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Reading and translating is the default, so the ruling seems unnecessary.

steps.title: We might have worried about דוד's honor
steps.stepSummary: We might have hidden these stories to protect דוד המלך's honor. The ברייתא teaches that they are read anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: let us worry about the honor of דוד. So it teaches us that they are read.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that these shameful events in דוד's family could embarrass him, so we might have skipped them. The ברייתא says they are read and translated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is no longer about the listeners. It is about the honor of a great figure, דוד המלך. Even so, his honor does not cause these stories to be skipped.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Let us be concerned.' Another form of נֵיחוּשׁ.
דוד המלך, the father of אמנון, תמר, and אבשלום.

phrases.english: let us be concerned for the honor of David,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: identifies a possible worry that the ruling rejects.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Skip the stories to protect דוד's honor.
steps.terutzMaskana: They are read and translated anyway.

steps.title: The story of פילגש בגבעה is read and translated
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that the story of פילגש בגבעה is read and translated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The story of the concubine in גבעה is read and translated.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives its next ruling: the terrible story at the end of ספר שופטים is read and translated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this story, people of the city of גבעה in שבט בנימין committed a horrible crime, and it led to a civil war against that tribe. The ruling is that the story is still presented to the public.

keyTerms.meaning: A city in the territory of שבט בנימין.

phrases.english: The incident of the concubine in Gibeah

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The story of פילגש בגבעה is read and translated.

steps.title: Why state this about פילגש בגבעה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: this is obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The same challenge is asked one more time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא looks for what we might have worried about that would justify skipping this story.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 20.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Reading and translating is the default, so the ruling seems unnecessary.

steps.title: We might have worried about the honor of שבט בנימין
steps.stepSummary: We might have hidden the story to protect the honor of שבט בנימין. The ברייתא teaches that it is read anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: let us worry about the honor of בנימין. So it teaches us that it is read.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the story shames an entire tribe, so we might have skipped it. The ברייתא rules that it is read and translated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the honor in question belongs to a whole שבט, not one person. Even so, it does not override reading the passage.

keyTerms.meaning: His honor. Here it means the tribe's honor.
שבט בנימין, the tribe whose members were involved in the story.

steps.whatToRemember: There are four more cases of the same pattern: ruling, then פשיטא, then מהו דתימא, then קא משמע לן. Worries about upsetting the ציבור, about people serving ה׳ out of fear, about דוד's honor, and about שבט בנימין's honor are all rejected. All of these passages are read and translated.

phrases.english: let us be concerned for the honor of Benjamin,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: identifies a possible worry that the ruling rejects.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Skip the story to protect שבט בנימין's honor.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is read and translated anyway.

steps.title: יחזקאל's rebuke of ירושלים is read and translated
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that יחזקאל's harsh rebuke of ירושלים is read as a הפטרה and translated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The passage 'Make known to ירושלים her abominations' is read and translated.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds another item to its list. יחזקאל's sharp rebuke of ירושלים may be read and translated in public.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This chapter of יחזקאל describes the sins of ירושלים very harshly. One might think it is too embarrassing for the public to hear. The ברייתא says it is still read and translated.

phrases.notes: יחזקאל טז:ב

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא's list of passages that are read and translated
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The passage of 'הודע את ירושלים' is read publicly and translated.

steps.title: Why would we need to say this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why this ruling needs to be stated at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ruling. It asks why we would ever think a passage of נביא could not be read.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same pattern as the earlier steps. Unless there is a reason to hide a passage, of course it is read and translated, so the ruling seems to teach nothing new.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the ruling in step 23
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that 'הודע את ירושלים' is read and translated
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A passage from נביא is normally read, so there is no reason to state this rule.

steps.title: The ruling rejects the view of רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: The ruling is needed to reject רבי אליעזר, who did not allow this passage to be read.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to exclude the view of רבי אליעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ruling is not obvious. There was a תנא, רבי אליעזר, who held that this passage should not be read.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since a real opinion forbade reading it, the ברייתא had to state clearly that the halacha is not like him. The passage is read and translated.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who objected to reading this passage

phrases.english: To exclude the view of Rabbi Eliezer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 24
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies an opposing opinion that the ruling comes to reject
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Following רבי אליעזר, one might think this passage should not be read.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא rejects רבי אליעזר. The passage is read and translated.

steps.title: The story showing רבי אליעזר's objection
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells how רבי אליעזר rebuked a man for reading this passage, and the man turned out to have a flaw in his lineage.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught: A man was reading 'Make known to ירושלים her abominations' in front of רבי אליעזר. רבי אליעזר said to him: Before you examine the abominations of ירושלים, go examine the abominations of your mother. They checked his family and found a trace of a lineage flaw.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source showing that רבי אליעזר really did object to reading this passage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר saw reading this passage as disrespect to ירושלים. His sharp comment turned out to be true, since the reader's mother had sinned. The story proves that the opinion step 25 mentioned really exists.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is taught in a ברייתא
A trace of a lineage flaw

steps.confusionAlert: The halacha does not follow רבי אליעזר. The story shows his view existed, but the ברייתא still rules that the passage is read and translated.

phrases.english: An incident with a certain man
who was reading in front of Rabbi Eliezer
Before you examine the abominations of Jerusalem,
go and examine the abominations of your mother.
and found in him a trace of a lineage flaw.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source for רבי אליעזר's view mentioned in step 25
steps.raayaObject: That רבי אליעזר objected to reading 'הודע את ירושלים'
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא telling of רבי אליעזר's rebuke of a reader

steps.title: New category: read but not translated, starting with ראובן
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא opens a new list of passages that are read but not translated. It gives the mnemonic רעבד"ן, and its first item is the incident of ראובן.
steps.simpleTranslation: And these are read but not translated (mnemonic: רעבד"ן). The incident of ראובן is read but not translated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now starts a new list. These passages are read aloud in Hebrew but not translated for the public. The first is ראובן and בלהה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the reading itself is kept, but the translation is skipped so the embarrassing content is less understood by everyone. The mnemonic רעבד"ן previews the items: ר for ראובן, ע for עגל, and so on.

keyTerms.meaning: The incident of ראובן with בלהה

steps.confusionAlert: This is a different category from before. Earlier passages were both read and translated. These are read in Hebrew only, with no translation.

phrases.english: And these are read but not translated,
The incident of Reuben is read but not translated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the 'read and translated' list to a new 'read but not translated' list
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The incident of ראובן and בלהה is read but not translated.

steps.title: רבי חנינא בן גמליאל stops the translation
steps.stepSummary: A story shows the rule in practice: רבי חנינא בן גמליאל told the translator to translate only the end of the ראובן verse, and the חכמים praised him.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an incident where רבי חנינא בן גמליאל went to כבול. The חזן was reading 'And it came to pass, while ישראל dwelt', and he said to the translator: Stop! Translate only the last part. The חכמים praised him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story that supports the rule about ראובן's incident.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חזן read the verse about ראובן aloud. רבי חנינא let the reading continue but blocked the translation of the embarrassing part. The praise of the חכמים confirms that this is the correct practice.

phrases.english: And there was an incident with Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel
and the synagogue attendant was reading
"And it came to pass, while Israel dwelt",
and he said to the translator:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the rule of step 27 being applied
steps.raayaObject: That ראובן's incident is read but not translated
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of רבי חנינא בן גמליאל in כבול, praised by the חכמים

steps.title: The second account of the עגל is read but not translated
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that the second account of the עגל is read but not translated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The second incident of the calf is read but not translated.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the next item on the 'read but not translated' list, the letter ע in the mnemonic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Not the whole story of the עגל is left untranslated, only a 'second' section of it. The גמרא will next explain exactly which section is meant.

keyTerms.meaning: The second account of the עגל הזהב

phrases.english: The second incident of the calf

steps.triggerLanguage: מַעֲשֵׂה עֵגֶל הַשֵּׁנִי נִקְרָא וְלֹא מִתַּרְגֵּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the רעבד"ן list
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The second account of the עגל is read but not translated.

steps.title: Which part is the second account?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which section counts as the 'second' account of the עגל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which is the second incident of the calf?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question to pin down which verses the rule is talking about. It is setting up the answer that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is unclear without defining 'second', since the עגל story has several parts. The question is about where the passage begins and ends.

phrases.english: Which is the second incident of the calf?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the definition of the term in step 29
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which verses make up the 'second account' of the עגל

steps.title: From 'ויאמר משה' until 'וירא משה'
steps.stepSummary: The second account is אהרן's conversation with משה, from 'ויאמר משה' until 'וירא משה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: From 'And משה said' until 'And משה saw'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by marking the exact verses. This is the section where משה questions אהרן and אהרן explains what happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The section runs from שמות לב:כא to לב:כה. It is called 'second' because it retells the עגל story, this time through אהרן's own words.

phrases.notes: שמות לב:כא
שמות לב:כה

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the שאלה of step 30
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The second account is אהרן's explanation to משה, שמות לב:כא–כה.

steps.title: Be careful with your answers: אהרן's words gave heretics an opening
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר teaches that a person must choose his words carefully. אהרן's answer that the calf 'came out' of the fire let the מינין deny their faith.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is taught: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: A person should always be careful with his answers. Because of the answer אהרן gave משה, the heretics broke away from faith, as it says: 'And I cast it into the fire, and this calf came out.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that connects to אהרן's answer. It helps explain why this section is sensitive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אהרן said the calf 'came out' of the fire, which sounds as though it formed by itself with some power of its own. The מינין used this phrasing to deny faith. The lesson is that a careless explanation can do more damage than the original act.

keyTerms.meaning: They broke away from faith / became heretical
And I cast it into the fire

steps.whatToRemember: There are two lists. Some sensitive passages are read and translated (for example 'הודע את ירושלים', against רבי אליעזר). Others are read but not translated (רעבד"ן: ראובן, the second account of the עגל, and more). The second עגל account is sensitive because אהרן's wording could be misused.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains the reason the second עגל section is not translated: אהרן's words, heard in the common language, could mislead listeners into thinking the calf had real power.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It is taught: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
A person should always be careful with his answers,
for because of the answer that Aaron gave Moses
the heretics broke away from faith,
"And I cast it into the fire, and this calf came out."
phrases.notes: שמות לב:כד

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר: לְעוֹלָם יְהֵא אָדָם זָהִיר בִּתְשׁוּבוֹתָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives background on why אהרן's answer in the section defined in step 31 is sensitive
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person must be careful with his answers. אהרן's wording 'and this calf came out' gave the מינין grounds to deny their faith.

steps.title: ברכת כהנים is read but not translated
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that ברכת כהנים is read in the Torah reading but not translated for the public.
steps.simpleTranslation: ברכת כהנים is read, but it is not translated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings up the next item from the משנה's list: ברכת כהנים is read but not translated. This sets up the question that comes next: why?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In those days, a translator (מתורגמן) translated the Torah reading into Aramaic so everyone could understand. Here the Hebrew is read, but the translator stays silent. The next two steps give the reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Are read (in Hebrew, from the Torah)
Are translated (into Aramaic for the listeners)

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next passage in the משנה's list of sensitive readings
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ברכת כהנים is read but not translated.

steps.title: Why is ברכת כהנים not translated
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind not translating ברכת כהנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why ברכת כהנים should not be translated. It is a beautiful blessing, so the rule seems surprising.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a plain request for a reason, not an attack on the rule. The answer will point to a specific word in the פסוק.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the rule in step 33
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why ברכת כהנים is not translated publicly

steps.title: Because the verse says God will 'lift up' His face
steps.stepSummary: The reason is the word 'ישא'. People might misunderstand it to mean that ה׳ plays favorites with the Jewish people.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it is written: 'May He lift up (His face to you).'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word 'ישא' ('ישא ה׳ פניו אליך') is the problem. A simple listener could misunderstand it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Lifting the face' sounds like showing special favor. Another פסוק says ה׳‎ 'לא ישא פנים', meaning He does not play favorites. A translation heard by unlearned people could make it sound as if ה׳ is unfair, so the translator stays silent.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Will lift up' (His face), meaning will show favor

phrases.notes: במדבר ו:כו. It could sound like favoritism, which seems to clash with 'לא ישא פנים' (דברים י:יז).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 34
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'ישא' could be misunderstood as ה׳ showing unfair favoritism.

steps.title: The story of דוד and אמנון is neither read nor translated
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: the story of דוד and אמנון is not read publicly and not translated.
steps.simpleTranslation: The incident of דוד and אמנון is neither read nor translated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next item in the משנה. The story of אמנון and his father דוד is not read at all and not translated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This rule is stricter than the earlier ones, because even the Hebrew reading is not done. The story is embarrassing for דוד המלך's family.

keyTerms.meaning: The incident of דוד and his son אמנון (with תמר), in שמואל ב פרק יג

phrases.english: The incident of David and Amnon

steps.triggerLanguage: מַעֲשֵׂה דָּוִד וְאַמְנוֹן לֹא נִקְרִין וְלֹא מִתַּרְגְּמִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the משנה's list
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The story of דוד and אמנון is neither read nor translated.

steps.title: But another source says אמנון and תמר is read and translated
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out a contradiction: an earlier source (the ברייתא/תוספתא) said the story of אמנון and תמר is both read and translated.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't you say that the incident of אמנון and תמר is read and translated?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה. Another source already ruled that the story of אמנון and תמר is read and translated, which seems to be the very same story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two sources seem to give opposite rulings about the same passage. One says it is not read at all, and the other says it is read and even translated. The גמרא needs to explain how both can be true.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't you say? (introduces a contradiction)

phrases.english: that the incident of Amnon and Tamar is read and translated?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the rule in step 36 using an earlier source
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that the story of דוד and אמנון is not read
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another source rules that the same story (אמנון and תמר) is read and translated.

steps.title: It depends on whether the verse says 'אמנון בן דוד'
steps.stepSummary: No contradiction: verses that call him 'אמנון בן דוד' are not read, while verses that just say 'אמנון' are read and translated.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This (not read) is where it is written 'אמנון בן דוד'; that (read) is where it is written just 'אמנון'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by splitting the story into two kinds of verses. Where the פסוק mentions דוד as אמנון's father, it is skipped. Where it just says 'אמנון', it is read.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The concern is protecting דוד's honor. Linking the shameful act directly to דוד ('בן דוד') is what makes the passage too embarrassing to read. So the two sources are talking about different פסוקים within the same story.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult (the two sources deal with different cases)

phrases.english: this is where it is written "Amnon son of David"
phrases.notes: Here the passage is not read, out of respect for דוד.

phrases.english: that is where it is written simply "Amnon".
phrases.notes: Here the passage is read and translated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 37
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source refers to different verses
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources seemed to rule on the same exact passage.
steps.terutzMaskana: Verses saying 'אמנון בן דוד' are skipped; verses saying just 'אמנון' are read and translated.
steps.whatToRemember: The concern is דוד's honor. Only verses that tie the act to 'בן דוד' are skipped.

steps.title: Coarse words in verses are read aloud with refined words
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that verses written with crude language are read publicly using cleaner words, and it gives examples.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: All verses written in the Torah in a coarse way are read in a refined way. For example: 'ישגלנה' is read 'ישכבנה'; 'עפולים' is read 'טחורים'; 'חריונים' is read 'דביונים'; 'to eat their dung and drink their urine' (crude words) is read with polite words for dung and urine; 'למחראות' is read 'למוצאות'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא with a general rule. When a פסוק uses a crude word, we read it aloud with a more polite word, and the ברייתא lists examples.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The written text stays exactly as it is, but the word spoken aloud is changed to a cleaner one. Each example pairs the crude written word with its polite reading. 'בתורה' here means all of תנ״ך, since most examples come from נביאים.

keyTerms.meaning: In a coarse or indecent way

steps.confusionAlert: Nobody changes the letters in the ספר. The written word (כתיב) stays, and only the spoken reading (קרי) is the polite word. This is the source of many קרי/כתיב notes in תנ״ך.

phrases.english: All the verses written in the Torah in a coarse way —
are read in a refined way, for example:
"yishgalena" (crude: will ravish her) is read "yishkavena" (will lie with her),
phrases.notes: דברים כח:ל
דברים כח:כז
מלכים ב ו:כה
מלכים ב יח:כז

phrases.english: is read: to eat their excrement (polite word)
and drink the 'water of their feet' (polite word for urine).

phrases.notes: מלכים ב י:כז, describing the temple of the בעל turned into a latrine.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: כׇּל הַמִּקְרָאוֹת הַכְּתוּבִין בַּתּוֹרָה לִגְנַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New ברייתא on a related theme: how sensitive passages are read publicly
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Coarse words in פסוקים are read aloud with refined substitutes.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן קרחה: mocking idols may be read as written
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן קרחה disagrees about 'למחראות'. Because it is used to shame עבודה זרה, it is read exactly as written.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן קרחה says: 'למחראות' is read as written, because it is a disgrace to עבודה זרה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן קרחה disagrees with the last example of the ברייתא. He says the crude word 'למחראות' is read as is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He accepts the general rule but makes an exception. When the crude word is used to mock עבודה זרה, the crudeness is the whole point and is allowed. Shaming idolatry is a good thing, so there is no need to soften it.

keyTerms.meaning: As they are written (literally 'as their name')

steps.whatToRemember: General rule: crude words are read politely. Exception (רבי יהושע בן קרחה): crude language used to mock עבודה זרה may be read as written.

phrases.english: because it is a disgrace to idol worship.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A dissenting view on the last example of the ברייתא in step 39
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Crude words used to mock עבודה זרה are read as written.

steps.title: רב נחמן: All mockery is forbidden except mockery of idols
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that all ליצנות is forbidden, except mocking עבודה זרה, which is permitted. His proof is from ישעיה, where the נביא mocks the idols בל and נבו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: All mockery is forbidden, except mockery of עבודה זרה, which is allowed. As it is written: 'בל bows down, נבו stoops.' And it is written: 'They stoop, they bow down together; they could not hold in the burden.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן turns רבי יהושע בן קרחה's point into a general rule: mocking anything is forbidden, but mocking עבודה זרה is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוקים describe the idols 'bowing' and 'stooping' as if squatting to relieve themselves, and being unable to hold in their 'burden.' Since the נביא himself mocks idols in crude terms, we learn that such mockery is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Burden; here read as the idol's 'load' that it cannot hold in

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the general rule behind the earlier ruling that 'למחראות' is read as written: shaming עבודה זרה is the one area where crude mockery is allowed.

phrases.english: except for mockery of idol worship, which is permitted.
As it is written: 'Bel bows down, Nevo stoops,'
phrases.notes: ישעיה 46:1. Pictured as squatting to relieve themselves.

phrases.english: and it is written: 'They stoop, they bow down together;
they could not hold back the burden, etc.'
phrases.notes: ישעיה 46:2.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: כֹּל לֵיצָנוּתָא אֲסִירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Broadens רבי יהושע בן קרחה's specific point about 'למחראות' into a general rule about mockery.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All mockery is forbidden except mockery of עבודה זרה, which is permitted, as shown from ישעיה 46.

steps.title: רבי ינאי's alternative source from הושע
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי brings a different source for permitting mockery of עבודה זרה: a פסוק in הושע about the calves of בית און, read with a wordplay, 'כבודו' as 'כבידו'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ינאי said: We learn it from here: 'The inhabitants of שומרון shall be in dread for the calves of בית און; for its people shall mourn over it, and its priests shall tremble for it, for its glory, because it has departed from it.' Do not read 'its glory' (כבודו), but rather 'its heavy load' (כבידו).
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ינאי agrees that mocking idols is allowed, but he proves it from a different פסוק in הושע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By reading 'כבודו' (its glory) as 'כבידו' (its heavy load), the פסוק mocks the golden calf as if its waste 'departed' from it. Since the פסוק itself mocks the idol, this shows that such mockery is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: The calves of Beth-aven (the golden calves set up by ירבעם)
Do not read it as ... but rather as ... (a wordplay reading)
Its heavy load, meaning its waste

steps.confusionAlert: 'אל תקרי' does not change the actual text of the פסוק. It is a way of drawing an extra lesson from the words.

phrases.english: 'The inhabitants of Samaria shall be in dread for the calves of Beth-aven,
for its people shall mourn over it,
and its priests shall tremble over it,
for its glory, because it has departed from it.'
phrases.notes: הושע 10:5.

phrases.english: Do not read 'its glory' (kevodo), but rather 'its heavy load' (keveido).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different pasuk as the source for רב נחמן's rule.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that mocking עבודה זרה is permitted.
steps.raayaSupportSource: הושע 10:5, reading 'כבודו' as 'כבידו', which mocks the calf idol.

steps.title: A Jew may tell a gentile to put his idol in a crude place
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר מנוח, in the name of רב אחא בריה דרב איקא, says a Jew may tell a גוי to take his idol and put it in his 'שין תיו', meaning his rear end.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בר מנוח said in the name of רב אחא בריה דרב איקא: A Jew is allowed to say to a גוי: Take your idol and put it in your 'שין תיו' (your rear end).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a practical example of the permission to mock עבודה זרה with crude language.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The letters 'שין תיו' spell 'שת', a word for the buttocks. Even here the גמרא hints at the word with letters instead of saying it outright, but the insult itself is permitted because it targets עבודה זרה.

keyTerms.meaning: The letters ש־ת, hinting at 'שֵׁת', the rear end

phrases.aramaic: מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא:
phrases.english: in the name of Rav Acha, son of Rav Ika:
It is permitted for a Jew
and place it in your 'shin-tav' (rear end).
phrases.notes: The letters ש and ת spell שת, which means buttocks.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בַּר מָנוֹחַ מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the permission to mock עבודה זרה to everyday speech.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A Jew may crudely mock a גוי's idol by telling him to put it in his rear end.

steps.title: Shaming someone with a bad reputation and praising someone with a good one
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says a person with a bad reputation may be shamed with the insult 'גימל שין'. A person with a good reputation may be praised, and whoever praises him receives blessings.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Someone whose reputation is bad, it is permitted to shame him with 'גימל שין.' Someone whose reputation is good, it is permitted to praise him, and whoever praises him, blessings will rest on his head.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי extends the topic from mocking idols to how we speak about people: shaming the openly wicked, and praising the good.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'גימל שין' is a coded insult (per רש"י, גירתא שריא, son of a foul harlot), allowed only against someone already known for bad behavior. The second half adds that publicly praising a good person is permitted and even brings blessing.

keyTerms.meaning: Coded letters for a harsh insult

steps.whatToRemember: Mockery is generally forbidden. The exceptions are mocking עבודה זרה and shaming a person with a known bad reputation. Praising good people is allowed and brings blessing.

phrases.english: it is permitted to shame him with 'gimel-shin',
phrases.notes: An acronym for a harsh insult.

phrases.english: it is permitted to praise him,
blessings will rest upon his head.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: הַאי מַאן דִּסְנֵי שׁוּמְעָנֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the exceptions to the ban on mockery from idols to people of bad reputation, and adds praise of good people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person with a bad reputation may be shamed with a coded insult. A person with a good reputation may be praised, and the one who praises him is blessed.

steps.title: הדרן — Closing the פרק הקורא את המגילה עומד
steps.stepSummary: The closing formula for the third perek of מגילה, הקורא את המגילה עומד.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, 'One who reads the מגילה standing.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא formally ends the פרק with the traditional הדרן, expressing the hope to come back and learn it again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not part of the halachic discussion. It marks a boundary, so the next line begins a brand-new פרק.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you (said at the end of a perek)
The name of the perek just finished

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ הַקּוֹרֵא אֶת הַמְּגִילָּה עוֹמֵד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the perek after רב אשי's final statement.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The third perek of מגילה is complete.

steps.title: New perek: selling holy items only to buy something holier
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה (פרק בני העיר) teaches that if a town sells a holy item, the money must be used to buy something of greater holiness: town square → בית הכנסת → תיבה → wrapping cloths → (continues).
steps.simpleTranslation: Residents of a town who sold the town square may use its money to buy a synagogue. If they sold a synagogue, they may buy an ark. If they sold an ark, they may buy wrapping cloths for ספרים. If they sold wrapping cloths...
steps.whatsHappening: A new פרק opens with a משנה listing a ladder of holiness: the proceeds from selling a holy item may only go 'up' to something holier. The list continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The town square has some holiness because people sometimes prayed there on fast days. Each item on the list is holier because it is closer to the ספר תורה itself: בית הכנסת, then the תיבה that holds it, then the cloths that wrap it directly.

keyTerms.meaning: Residents of the town (also the name of the new פרק)
Wrapping cloths for the ספר תורה

steps.confusionAlert: The משנה is not saying you must buy these items. It says that if you sell a holy item, its money may only be used for something holier, never for something lower.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basic rule of מעלין בקודש: holiness may go up but not down. It governs the sale of בתי כנסיות and תשמישי קדושה.

phrases.aramaic: בְּנֵי הָעִיר שֶׁמָּכְרוּ רְחוֹבָהּ שֶׁל עִיר —
phrases.english: Residents of a town who sold the town square,
may buy a synagogue with its proceeds.
If they sold a synagogue, they may buy an ark.
If they sold an ark, they may buy wrapping cloths.

phrases.notes: The משנה continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּנֵי הָעִיר שֶׁמָּכְרוּ רְחוֹבָהּ שֶׁל עִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new perek after the הדרן. It is unrelated to the previous discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Money from selling a holy item may only be used to buy something of greater holiness.
